elements.label: Hotter, drier summers
elements.description: Summers with less rain and more evaporation. Around 2050 (2036–2065), against 1991–2020, every KNMI'23 scenario has 2 to 13% less summer rain, 6 to 11% more potential evaporation in summer and a largest precipitation deficit of April to September 13 to 35% larger, and the great rivers carry less water in summer (KNMI, 2023, pp. 3–4, 42). Measured as national averages, evaporation over five stations, Vlissingen among them (p. 5): the scenarios give no rain or deficit figure for Zeeland. Set outside the island: a Constant.

elements.label: Sea-level rise
elements.description: The mean level of the sea at the Dutch coast. Around 2050 (2036–2065) every KNMI'23 scenario has it 16 to 38 cm above 1995–2014, 24 cm in the low-emission scenarios and 27 cm in the high, still rising by 1 to 8 mm a year (KNMI, 2023, pp. 3, 5). Set outside the island: a Constant.

elements.label: Wetter winters
elements.description: More rain in winter. Around 2050 (2036–2065), against 1991–2020, every KNMI'23 scenario has 4 to 7% more winter rain, and 0.4 to 0.8 more days a winter with 10 mm or more (KNMI, 2023, p. 3). Measured as a national average over 13 rain stations (p. 5): the scenarios give no figure for Zeeland. Set outside the island: a Constant.

elements.label: Rainwater lens recharge in the low polders
elements.description: The rain that soaks in and refills the rainwater lenses of the low polders: mostly the winter's rain surplus, since in summer most of the rain evaporates (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 155, for the Netherlands). On Schouwen-Duiveland upward saline seepage keeps it within the clay top layer of the low polders, and tile drains carry much of it off during each rain; recharge, seepage and drainage depth together set the lens's thickness (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3661–3662, 3673–3675, measured on the island).

elements.label: Rainwater lens thickness in the low polders
elements.description: The thickness of the fresh rainwater lenses on top of the saline groundwater in the island's low polders, from the surface to the middle of the mixing zone between them: about 2 m on average in the low-lying polders with saline seepage, under 2 m over more than half of the 56 km² surveyed (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3667, 3672–3673, 3675, measured on the island from a helicopter and on the ground). These lenses keep salt out of the root zone and reach only the crop on their own field. A Stock: a year's recharge barely moves it (Rainwater lens recharge in the low polders → Rainwater lens thickness in the low polders).

elements.label: Land subsidence
elements.description: How fast the land surface of the island's polders falls. Peat above the groundwater compacts and its organic matter oxidises as it is drained (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 13, the board's rules for its whole area), and the fall adds up in Polder surface elevation. The island's low polders lie on peat: in Schouwen's low polder salt-marsh soils alternate with basin clay with peat (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 23), and under Duiveland a peat layer lies almost everywhere at −1.6 to −3.4 m NAP, under calcareous sand or light clay (2021a, p. 20), often within a metre of the surface in its low south and middle (p. 19). Drained by ditches, the polders have sunk over several hundred years as the peat compacted and the clay ripened (2021b, pp. 20, 22; 2021a, p. 18). No source read gives the rate on the island. The rate follows the drainage within the year, so an Auxiliary; what builds up slowly is the elevation, a Stock.

ask actors.for: How fast the island's polders subside, per area: the board changes a level in soil prone to settling by no more than the land has subsided since (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 50).

elements.label: Polder surface elevation (NAP)
elements.description: The land surface elevation of the island's polders relative to NAP, lowered by subsidence: most of the low polders' surface lies around NAP (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10), the western low polders mostly between −1 and −2 m NAP and the eastern ones at about 0 to +1 m (pp. 27–28), the middle and east of Schouwen between −1.5 and −0.5 m NAP (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 22), and the lowest polders at −1.5 to −2.5 m below mean sea level (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3661). Tidal silt, let in through a wisselpolder, would barely raise it on this island: the Grevelingen has no tide, and the Oosterschelde has too little silt to raise polders on a large scale (De Mesel et al., 2013). Since the storm surge barrier its channels carry 52–70% less suspended sediment (Ma et al., 2014, p. 15); near Zierikzee the water holds under 10 mg/l, mostly fine sand, and its salt marshes rise 3–10 mm a year (van Maldegem & de Jong, 2004, pp. 14, 27), against 16–32 mm on young marshes along the Westerschelde (De Mesel et al., 2013).

elements.label: Root zone salinity
elements.description: The salt concentration of the soil water in the crop root zone. Salt harms a crop in two phases: at once osmotically, slowing the growth of young leaves, and more slowly as sodium (Na+) or chloride (Cl-) builds up in the leaves, ageing the older ones early (Munns & Tester, 2008, pp. 654–656, a review of plant physiology, which holds wherever the crop grows). It rises in a dry summer as the soil dries out and salt rises by capillary rise, and falls with the winter's rain surplus, which washes the topsoil of well-drained soil free of salt in one winter and that of badly drained soil in two or three (van Beekom et al., 1953a, pp. 155–158, measured after the floods in Zeeland): within the year where the soil drains well, so an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Saline seepage (kwel)
elements.description: The upward flow of salt groundwater from the sand below into the clay and peat top layer of the island's polders, in mm a day, which leaves through drains, ditches and evaporation (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3662). The higher water pressure at depth drives it in the low polders, where it keeps the rainwater lenses thin, mostly under 2 m, and the shallow groundwater brackish to salt (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10); below the lens its water holds 10 to 16 g of chloride a litre (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675), against about 16 to 17 g in North Sea water (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). Most of Duiveland gets salt seepage, most in its low parts near the Oosterschelde (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 27); in the western low polders it is strongest near the Grevelingen and the Oosterschelde (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27). The flow follows the water pressures, which change constantly with recharge and drainage (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675): within the year, so an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Soil structure
elements.description: The soil's aggregates and pores, which set how fast water soaks in: well-drained clay with its structure intact let the winter's rain surplus soak through almost completely, while clay whose structure sodium had broken down became impervious and sticky when wet (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 157; 1953b, pp. 230, 233, measured after the floods in Zeeland). A Stock: once broken down, it recovers over years (Root zone salinity → Soil structure). Workability, which structure and wetness both shape, is Spring workability of the fields.

elements.label: Upconing of salt groundwater
elements.description: The rise of salt groundwater towards a well that pumps fresh water from a lens floating on it, in a cone under the well. In Zeeland fresh groundwater is mostly pumped through horizontal wells, under rules meant to limit this upconing and salt intrusion (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 1). In the Freshmaker pilot on a creek ridge at Ovezande, Zuid-Beveland, the pumped water grew saltier during each pumping season, as the lens thinned and the cone reached the shallow well (p. 67); in a model of the creek ridge at Serooskerke, Walcheren, the cone had not settled after ten years (p. 58), the slow part being the lens itself (Freshwater lens thickness under creek ridges, a Stock). The island's creek ridges hold the same kind of lens, rain soaked in over salt groundwater (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). Deltares, modelling Zeeland's rules in 2018, found them on the whole enough to prevent strong salinisation under and around a well (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021, p. 1). Within the season: an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Farmers' demand for deep polder drainage
elements.description: Farmers' wish for low ditch levels, so that their fields drain: dry enough in spring for heavy machinery to work them, which holding water back for dry times makes hard (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021c, p. 44), and free of water damage after heavy rain, which farmers in the island's western low polders often find a bigger problem than drought (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27). They put it to the water board as it prepares its water level plans, which it does with interest groups such as farming, and in views on a draft (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 17): on Duiveland's draft of 2021, four views feared that a raise the plan proposed to study would bring more flooding in extreme rain (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 53). Within the year, so an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Fresh water supplied to the island
elements.description: Fresh water brought to the island's farms from outside it in the growing season (present in Tholen and Zeeuws-Vlaanderen; absent on Walcheren, the Bevelanden and Schouwen-Duiveland). It needs a supply route, and in drought it is what the national distribution leaves for the route to carry. Rijkswaterstaat makes that distribution: in drought it divides the little fresh water of the large rivers and lakes among the users through weirs, pumping stations and sluices, by the verdringingsreeks when there is too little for all, and the greater part of Zeeland lies outside the area it can supply (Rijkswaterstaat, n.d.).

elements.label: Freshwater availability for crops
elements.description: Fresh water crops can draw on in the growing season: rain, the soil moisture and groundwater of the field above the lens, water farmers pump or have stored, and water supplied from outside, which reaches the island nowhere now (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 4, 8). A Stock: water held in the root zone and in storage carries over from day to day: the root zone's is a daily balance, what the day before left plus rain, irrigation and capillary rise, less what the crop uses and what drains below the roots (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8, eq. 85). It fills and empties within the season.

elements.label: Freshwater storage measures
elements.description: The fresh water a year that the measures in place on the island's farms keep, store or collect for the growing season. They work three ways (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 16–23, 53, for the island): in the low polders, controlled drainage, anti-salinisation drainage (Drains2Buffer) and weirs in ditches keep the thin rainwater lens against salt, the water staying in the field's own soil, where it cannot be pumped (pp. 33, 53); on the creek ridges, the dunes and where a sand layer lies under the clay, the creek-ridge infiltration system, the Freshmaker and underground storage under a clay layer infiltrate winter water to pump in summer (pp. 20–22, 38); and double drainage collects fresh drain water into a basin to irrigate from (pp. 23, 29, 32). An adaptive practice: measures to keep more fresh water in the ground as drought and salinisation increase (p. 4). The study found them not yet fitted to the island and too risky for many farms to invest in alone (pp. 4, 11). A Stock: a measure, once built, lasts 15 to 30 years (pp. 17–22, 34). The farm decides a measure; infiltrating water needs the water board's permit or a notification, a weir the neighbours' consent, and raising a ditch's level the water board's cooperation (pp. 26, 44–45). Whether a farm wants to store weighs storing against its other ways through a dry summer (pumping, other crops), where capacity to invest is whether it can. Stored water pays back over years, which suits a farm that owns its land more than one on a short lease; and where stored water spreads under the neighbours, one farm pays and others gain. Whether either holds a farm back is a question for the group model building session. Beside the farms, Acacia Water, Deltares and Delphy shape it: in a demonstration with the trial farm Rusthoeve and the municipality, double drainage was laid on two test plots at Kerkwerve and anti-salinisation drainage on one at Dreischor, on three of the island's farms (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, 2023), the EU's rural development programme paying half of the cost and the knowledge parties a part of it (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, n.d.-b).
elements.simplification: Counts the measures of three kinds as one quantity, the fresh water a year they keep, store or collect, each kind reaching crops by its own link out: to Winter rain drained away, to Freshwater lens thickness under creek ridges and dunes, and to Freshwater availability for crops. It assumes every kind responds alike to the drivers into this element. Every loop through it keeps its polarity and its mechanism; what it leaves out is that a rise in one kind need not be a rise in another, so the semi-quantitative analysis cannot vary them apart.

elements.label: Groundwater extraction for irrigation
elements.description: Fresh water farmers pump from the fresh groundwater through their own wells, to irrigate in summer; the water board's pumping stations belong to drainage. How much and from where is Pumping the water board allows. Whose lens a well draws on, the farm's own or one it shares with its neighbours, so that a farm pumping less leaves water to them, is a hypothesis for the group model building session; the rules are written so that a well's effects stay within the farm's own field (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021), an aim of the rules rather than a measurement. Pumping follows the season's shortfall within the year: an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Objections to land-use plans
elements.description: The views and appeals against the plans for the island's water and land while a plan is pending, the water board's level plans among them, which can slow, change or stop it. On a level plan, the views come in the six weeks its draft lies open and are answered in the decision, and anyone affected may appeal at the court for six weeks after it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 17–18). No source read gives the routes for the other bodies' plans.

elements.label: Winter rain drained away
elements.description: Rain in winter that field drains carry off instead of refilling the rainwater lens: in the low polders tile drains carry much of it off during each rain (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3661–3662, 3673–3675, measured on the island). It follows each rain, within the year: an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Crop yield
elements.description: Physical yield per hectare of conventional crops (potatoes, onions, sugar beet) under the prevailing freshwater, soil and workability conditions; what salt takes from their harvest is Harvest lost to salt. The island's arable farms grow potatoes, onions, sugar beet, cereals, grass seed and vegetables in rotation (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 30, 38, from the farms studied), and some in the low polders have stopped growing sown onions for the salt (p. 31). A season's harvest: an Auxiliary.
elements.simplification: The current crops (potatoes, onions, sugar beet) are one yield per hectare. Each yields less with a larger water shortfall, worse soil structure or fields that cannot be worked in time, so every link into the yield keeps its sign for each crop and no loop through it changes. What one yield leaves out: the crops lose in different proportions (the yield response factors on Crop water shortfall → Crop yield), and farms can shift their rotation among them, as some in the low polders stopped growing sown onions for the salt.

elements.label: Market demand for alternative crops
elements.description: Consumer demand and offtake contracts for novel salt-tolerant or alternative crops (e.g. protein crops). For quinoa the market is small: in Flanders it is sold under contract at €1,100 a tonne on a local market still very limited, with no forecast yet of how demand for local quinoa will grow (Cloet et al., 2024, pp. 2–3); in the Netherlands a supermarket has its own-brand quinoa from 12 Dutch farmers under a three-year contract, Dutch quinoa costing more to buy in than imported (DutchNews.nl, 2026). For protein crops, Rabobank expects demand for plant-based meat and dairy alternatives to grow towards 2030, while low yields and a quality that often misses food standards keep their price low (Polman et al., 2026, p. 8). For halophytes such as samphire and sea aster, grown in a few places in Zeeland, the food market is small and easily saturated, and offers farmers no lasting market potential (van den Burg et al., 2024, p. 6). Measured in Flanders, the Netherlands and Zeeland, none on the island.

elements.label: Local processing capacity for new crops
elements.description: Plants and supply chains on or near the island that store, process or sell new salt-tolerant crops. Breeding of tolerant varieties is Salt-tolerant varieties on offer. No source read shows a new crop processed on the island. Sea vegetables are sorted and packed by hand by a grower and trader at Nieuw- en Sint Joosland, who sells to restaurants and supermarkets at home and abroad and works with a colleague from Schouwen-Duiveland (FreshPlaza, 2018), its company growing at Colijnsplaat (EU CAP Network, 2023). Dutch quinoa's chain is run from Wageningen by GreenFood50, which has its quinoa grown close to its processing facilities (GreenFood50, n.d.), and a Zeeland quinoa chain was a project from 2021 to 2024 (De Vriend, 2024a). Buyers and processors build or keep it where they find it worthwhile against processing the crops elsewhere.

elements.label: Adoption of new salt-tolerant crops
elements.description: Hectares under crops new to the island's rotations that tolerate salt. The island's rotations hold potato, onion, sugar beet, cereals and grass seed (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 30), and no source read shows a new crop grown on the island. Elsewhere in Zeeland, most still experimental and small (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 57): samphire and sea aster, irrigated with saline water on the edges of salt marshes at Emmadorp, Waterdunen and Wolphaarsdijk, labour intensive and seasonal, their sales low (van den Burg et al., 2024, p. 6); sea fennel and sea banana on an arable farm at Colijnsplaat, where a new company worked out how to grow them, in fields and greenhouses, and set up their supply chain (EU CAP Network, 2023). Quinoa grows to maturity on irrigation water of more than 250 mM NaCl (van Loo, 2023, p. 77) and is sown with standard equipment and harvested with a combine, but needs a fine seed bed and weed control set by its row distance (p. 75). Farmers grow one where they find it worthwhile against their current crops; capacity to invest is whether they can, and dependence on the current crops what holds them. A Stock: a field keeps its crop through the season, and farmers move fields to a new crop over years, as they come to see the damage over dry summers (Harvest lost to salt → Adoption of new salt-tolerant crops).

elements.label: Agricultural land value
elements.description: The price unlet farmland on the island sells for (€/ha), set by what buyers expect to earn from it. A buyer bids at most what an extra hectare can earn back over the years of the investment (Farjon et al., 2013, p. 2), and the price is set for an important part by what expanding farms earn on extra hectares, their income and expectations combined with what they can borrow: scale enlargement and low interest rates hold it up, swings in what the land earns and limits on banks' financing of land press it down (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, pp. 1–3). So it has risen far faster than what the land earns on average, tenfold since 1970 against two to three times for net value added (Farjon et al., 2013, p. 1). Farmers bought 54% of the land traded in the Netherlands from 2012 to early 2023 and investors 9%, their segment among the most active in Zeeland, where just over 1.5% of the farmland changes hands in a year (Kuiper et al., 2023, pp. 1–2). Banks hold it as security for their loans (Farjon et al., 2013, p. 3). No source read gives the island's land prices.
elements.simplification: A soil's structure enters the land's value only through what the land earns (Soil structure → Crop yield → Farm income → this element), the sign the same, since buyers price what they expect it to earn. What it leaves out: any value a buyer gives good soil beyond its income.

elements.label: Risk premium on farm loans
elements.description: The part of a farm loan's interest that differs between clients: the specific premium a bank charges above the base rate, which banks also call the credit or risk premium. The loan's risk sets it for a large part: the interest holds, per client, the bank's expected losses on the loan and the cost of the capital the banks' solvency rules require it to hold against it, both higher the higher the credit risk the bank sees; on a loan with a fixed rate it may be part of one total rate (ABN AMRO, n.d.-a, n.d.-b). No source read gives the premiums banks charge the island's farms.

elements.label: Basel IV capital requirements
elements.description: The capital European rules require banks to hold against their loans, by the final Basel III standards. The EU sets them: its banking package (CRR III/CRD VI) puts the final elements of the Basel III standards of 2017 into EU law, the new rules of the Capital Requirements Regulation applying from 1 January 2025, those of the directive once each member state has transposed them; its output floor sets a lower limit on the capital requirements banks calculate with their own models; and environmental, social and governance risks enter the banks' handling of risk, the supervisors' annual review and disclosure (European Commission, Directorate-General for Financial Stability, Financial Services and Capital Markets Union, 2023). By the EBA's estimate, EU banks' minimum Tier 1 capital requirement is 9.0% higher at full implementation in 2028, the output floor and credit risk contributing most (European Banking Authority, 2023). No source read shows climate or salinisation risk in the risk weights of farm loans.

elements.label: Dependence on high-margin salt-sensitive crops
elements.description: The share of the rotation under the high-value cash crops salt harms most, seed and ware potatoes and sown onions (Root zone salinity → Harvest lost to salt). Potatoes are financially attractive and sensitive to the climate, the most important crop of Dutch arable farming (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 12): on specialised arable farms on clay they bring in 55% of the arable revenue, ware potatoes 32% and seed potatoes 23%, against 14% for onions and 11% for sugar beet (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 14). In Zeeland, a manager of the cooperative CZAV says, a farmer earns his money not with rotation crops but with onions, beets and potatoes (Economic Board Zeeland, 2023, p. 19). A field takes potatoes at most one year in three against soil disease, so a farm growing more of them rents or swaps land (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 4). The island's rotations hold potato, onion, sugar beet, cereals and grass seed; in its low polders, where the seepage pressure is high and the surface water salty all year, farmers have stopped growing sensitive crops such as sown onions, and with more fresh water they would be open to more profitable crops (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 30–31). In Zeeland the sown onions halved from 4,705 ha in 2019 to 2,579 in 2024 after dry summers, poor harvests and a lack of fresh water, which four in five arable farmers have no access to, while potatoes held at about 19,000 ha (De Vriend, 2024b). A Stock: the share holds through the season and shifts over years (Root zone salinity → Dependence on high-margin salt-sensitive crops).

elements.label: Farm income
elements.description: Farms' income from their crops: the revenue from crop sales, set by yield and prices, minus the costs they pay (rent, interest, the water board's levy, their own pumping) and depreciation, as Dutch farm accounts measure it (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 21), per hectare in a year. Dutch arable farms earned about 65,000 euro per unpaid labour unit on average over 2010–2016, spread widely: in 2016 a fifth had a negative income and as many earned more than 100,000 euro (pp. 21–22). In 2025 an estimated 60,000 euro, lower prices after good harvests in north-west Europe and beyond outweighing the yields (van der Meulen, 2025). No source read gives the island's farm incomes.

elements.label: Farmers' capacity to invest
elements.description: What a farm can put into an investment: its savings, built up from what is left of its income after the household's spending and its payment obligations, repayments included, and the credit a bank will give it. A farm whose income is negative cannot reserve enough for investment (Verhagen et al., 2018, pp. 23, 25), and one short of cash first cuts maintenance and private spending or draws on its savings, then asks its bank to defer interest and repayments or for more credit (p. 28); banks judge more and more whether a farm's operations earn enough to meet all its financial obligations (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19). Dutch arable farms invest mostly in machines, implements and installations (p. 19), and irrigation systems cost relatively much to install, not always within a farmer's reach (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 28).

elements.label: Financial leverage
elements.description: The farm's debt relative to the value of its assets, the inverse of its solvency (equity as a share of total capital). Land is 70% of an arable farm's balance sheet (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 13), so the ratio moves with the land price: arable farms' solvency was 81% in 2018 because their land had risen in value, while their long-term debt had tripled since 2001 to 770,000 euro per farm, and it differs widely between farms (p. 21). Farms that expanded recently have a lower solvency, about 70% on large arable farms in 2015 (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, p. 3); farms that own little of their land gain little from a rising land price but owe much less (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 26).

elements.label: Arable land in the polders
elements.description: Hectares of the island's land under arable crops, the census's akkerbouw, conventional or salt-tolerant and fallow included, whoever owns it: 9,094 ha in 2025 against 11,395 ha in 2000, on farms whose main seat is on the island (CBS, 2026). The farms growing them halved over those years, from 402 to 200, so the hectares per farm rose from 28 to 45: land from a farm that stops mostly goes in parts to neighbouring farms that are expanding, which can pay the most for it (Luijt, 2007, p. 25, nationally). The fall in hectares is net, the census's farmland 906 ha smaller and its grass and forage crops 1,431 ha larger (CBS, 2026). It falls when the land's holder, present or next, stops growing arable crops on it; what the land becomes then (nature, grassland, water storage) waits for the group's system boundary.

elements.label: Crop water shortfall
elements.description: What crops need in the growing season beyond the water they get: the gap farmers' water decisions respond to. What a crop needs, whatever the water's origin, is the water it uses when it has enough, its evapotranspiration, set by the weather (radiation, air temperature, humidity and wind speed) and by the crop and its stage of growth (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56, a guide to crop water use that holds wherever the crop grows). The island's farms depend wholly on rain and on the fresh groundwater under the dunes, the creek ridges and the thin rainwater lenses of the low polders; with no link to the main freshwater system, no fresh water can be brought in and no ditches flushed in dry periods, so the farms run short of water, as the dry years 2018, 2019 and 2020 showed (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8). It follows the weather within the season: an Auxiliary.

elements.label: ZLTO's call for a supply route
elements.description: How firmly ZLTO asks the province, the municipality and the water board for a route bringing fresh water to the island. After a report on the island's freshwater demand, its branch there called a pipeline from the Haringvliet the one solution (Omroep Zeeland, 2023), and its chair looks for more fresh water with the municipality and the province (van Essen, 2026). An Auxiliary: it follows the shortfall farmers report and holds nothing of its own.

elements.label: Freshwater supply route to the island
elements.description: Pipes or channels that could bring fresh water to the island, as their capacity in a summer; none exists. Provincie Zeeland, the actor here as the only body shown acting on the island's route, had a pipeline explored after the farming sector pressed for one (Witteveen+Bos, 2021, p. 7); the study leaves open who pays and who would run it (p. 51), and no source read shows a decision. By law a project decision can come from the water board's executive, for its water tasks, the province's or a minister (Omgevingswet, 2026, art. 5.44), and the water board may charge the farmland a supply project serves up to 100% more, once at least half of its owners have responded and two thirds of those are in favour (Waterschapswet, 2026, art. 122); it charges more for its supply projects on Tholen and Sint Philipsland and in the Reigersbergsche polder (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026c, arts. 5–6). IenW shapes it twice: its minister allots the Delta Fund, from which a freshwater region can claim 25% of a regional measure's cost, up to 50% for an innovative one or one carried out by several regions (Algemene Rekenkamer, 2026, p. 31); and the Delta Programme 2027, under the Delta Commissioner's direction and presented by the minister with the Delta Fund's budget, proposes that the south-west delta's areas with no supply from outside speed up their way to self-sufficiency, the region open to exploring small extensions of the supplied area that add evident value, are future-proof and keep the extra demand on the Volkerak-Zoommeer limited, the demand on the Hollandsch Diep and Haringvliet not raised (Ministerie van Infrastructuur en Waterstaat et al., 2026, pp. 88–89).

elements.label: Spring workability of the fields
elements.description: Whether heavy machinery can work the fields early in spring without damaging the soil, set by soil structure and by how wet the soil is: soil work done when the soil is too wet smears and compacts it and forms clods, and more rain in spring leaves fewer moments to do it (Verstand et al., 2021, p. 25, from the Dutch cultivation guides, on potatoes). It follows the soil's wetness within the season, so an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Polder drainage depth
elements.description: How far below the surface the water board holds the ditch levels in the island's polders (the drooglegging), as its water level plans set them: Duiveland's plan sets a target level for each of its level areas, from 0.8 to 2.7 m below NAP, in most the summer level higher than the winter one, against nature's order, to prevent water damage in winter and drying in summer (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 37, 63–64). It moves from the winter level to the summer one in steps in March and April, as the weather and the farmers' soil work allow (p. 66). On a creek ridge studied for water storage the depth is over 1.5 m in winter in large parts (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 42). The depth holds until the board carries out a new plan: Duiveland's plan of 2021 replaced one from 1982 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 24), and the board checks each plan every three years and renews it at 17 years or once it no longer fits (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 16–17), so a Stock. Where the land subsides under a level held, the depth shrinks until a new plan lowers the level, as the board has done where there is peat (2025, p. 13).

elements.label: Water board's plans to raise ditch levels
elements.description: The water level plans in which Waterschap Scheldestromen raises a polder's ditch levels, from the draft until their levels take effect. The board matches its levels to the land's use and soil, its principle that the level follows the land use: arable land 80 to 120 cm below the surface by soil, permanent grassland 20 cm less (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 29; 2025, pp. 5, 7), weighing flooding, drought, fresh water and groundwater (2021c, p. 19), subsidence (2025, pp. 13–14) and a change's costs against its benefits (2025, p. 12). On Duiveland the plan of 2021 proposed studying a raise in 14 level areas, where levels had been kept low to store extreme rain, to enlarge the fresh water in the soil and give crops more moisture (2021a, p. 69). The general board adopts each plan (2025, p. 18); of its 30 members, 26 represent the residents and two the owners of unbuilt land, farmland included, appointed by ZLTO's board (Reglement voor het Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, arts. 6–7). A plan waits years for the works its levels need (Water board's plans to raise ditch levels → Polder drainage depth), so a Stock.
elements.simplification: The two seats on the general board for the owners of unbuilt land, farmland included, were a Constant driving these plans, and are in the description instead: no loop runs through a Constant, so no loop changes. What it leaves out: the seats cannot be set as an input of their own.

elements.label: Water board's pumping costs
elements.description: What Waterschap Scheldestromen spends on electricity for the pumping stations that hold the polders' ditch levels, by pumping out the water that reaches the ditches. Every polder on the island is pumped: on Schouwen all water flows to two pumping stations, which pump it over the dike into the Oosterschelde and the Grevelingen (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 24); low-lying Duiveland has a pumping station for each of its five drainage areas (2021a, p. 21). Across the board's area the cost follows the water pumped: in the dry year 2025 its water systems spent €1.1 million less on electricity than budgeted, for the drought (2026e, p. 18), and for 2026 it budgets about €4.8 million for the electricity of its sewage and polder pumping stations together, which extreme rain can raise by up to 25% (p. 55). No source read gives the island's share. A year's spending: an Auxiliary.
elements.simplification: Draws only the water coming in: Saline seepage and Winter rain drained away, which Polder drainage depth and Polder surface elevation already drive with the same sign, so every loop keeps its polarity. What it leaves out: how high the water is lifted, on which no source read shows the costs depending.

ask actors.for: What its pumping stations on the island use in electricity a year, how much of the water they pump is seepage and how much rain, and how far the cost depends on how high they lift it: it measures the discharge at each pumping station (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 23).

elements.label: Water board levy on farmland
elements.description: What Waterschap Scheldestromen charges on farmland for its water management, pumping included. The law charges those who hold unbuilt land by ownership, possession or a limited right (Waterschapswet, 2026, art. 117), which leaves out its tenants, at one rate per hectare (art. 121): €115.53 for 2026 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026d, art. 6).

elements.label: Harvest lost to salt
elements.description: The conventional crops' harvest that salt in the root zone takes, over the island's fields still under them, in a season. On the island, farms where seepage pressure is high and the surface water is salty all year have stopped growing sensitive crops such as sown onions (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 31). Zeeland is among the coastal provinces where potatoes and barley lose considerable yield to salt (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 12). Salt's effect on yield builds up over weeks to months and is read over the season (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8): within the year, so an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Margin given up on high-margin crops
elements.description: On the hectares a farm moves from its high-margin current crops, potatoes and sown onions, to new salt-tolerant crops or to salt-tolerant varieties of the current crops: what the current crop would earn without salt less what the new crop or variety earns, a margin being revenue minus the crop's variable costs (Cloet et al., 2024, p. 1). What salt takes is Harvest lost to salt, so it is not counted here. Potatoes, beets, onions and field vegetables are the high-margin crops; the margin of protein crops is comparable to that of cereals and cannot compete with most other crops (Polman et al., 2026, p. 9); quinoa, in a study for Flanders, yields about 3 tonnes a hectare, sold at €1,100 a tonne under contract on a market still very small, against costs of about €1,470 a hectare (Cloet et al., 2024, pp. 2–3). In the Netherlands, interviews on quinoa and seed potatoes on saline soil found the lack of economic benefits the main constraint on scaling them (de Wit et al., 2022, p. 276), and on Terschelling food grown on salt-affected soil costs more to produce than food grown with fresh water, the project relying on volunteers and, at its start, on subsidies (ten Dam et al., 2023, pp. 10, 13, 16). A season's crop: within the year.

elements.label: Farms with a successor
elements.description: Arable farms on the island whose farmer has someone to take the farm over. Nationally, in 2023, 43% of the 33,000 farms whose head is over 50 had a successor, against 40% in 2020, and 39% of the arable farms, the agricultural census asking three times in ten years (Agrimatie, 2024); no source read gives the island's figure.

ask actors.for: How many arable farmers on the island over 50 have a successor.

elements.label: Harvest of new crops to process
elements.description: The volume of new salt-tolerant crops harvested in a year within reach of a processor or trader on or near the island, from the island's growers and from growers elsewhere. Quinoa has been grown in Zeeland since 2016, on one to four parcels a year at six locations in all (Bogers et al., 2025, pp. 28, 38), its map showing none on the island, while the growers who sell to GreenFood50 in the Netherlands farm about 200 hectares for 600 tonnes a year (DutchNews.nl, 2026); samphire is the main crop of a Zeeland grower and trader of sea vegetables (FreshPlaza, 2018).

elements.label: Net price for new crops after transport
elements.description: What farmers on the island get for new salt-tolerant crops once transport to the processor is paid, set by processors on and off the island. Quinoa fetches 0.70 to 1.25 euro a kilo at the farm gate (van Loo, 2023, p. 79), most Dutch growers selling it under contract to one buyer (DutchNews.nl, 2026). The food market for halophytes is small and easily saturated (van den Burg et al., 2024, p. 6), a Zeeland trader noting surpluses (FreshPlaza, 2018); no source read gives their price.

elements.label: Growers of new crops elsewhere
elements.description: Farmers off the island growing the same new crops, whose harvest a local plant could also process. More than two dozen farmers in the Netherlands grow quinoa, most under contract with GreenFood50, together working about 200 hectares for 600 tonnes a year, one of them at Vierhuizen in Groningen, and a few independently (DutchNews.nl, 2026); GreenFood50 has had it grown in the Netherlands and Belgium since 2014 (GreenFood50, n.d.).

elements.label: Processing of new crops elsewhere
elements.description: Plants off the island that buy and process new salt-tolerant crops: where the island's growers can sell a new crop now, beside a local plant. For Dutch quinoa the sources read show one main buyer, GreenFood50 at Wageningen, which runs the chain from grower to customer and has its quinoa grown close to its processing facilities, which it does not locate (GreenFood50, n.d.), most Dutch growers under contract with it (DutchNews.nl, 2026).

elements.label: Adoption of salt-tolerant varieties
elements.description: Hectares under salt-tolerant varieties of the current crops (potato, onion), which use the same machines, storage and know-how. Farmers grow one where they find it worthwhile against the variety they grow now. Such potato varieties exist and are tested in the Netherlands: of 13 cultivars from Dutch breeders and suppliers grown in the field on Texel from 2012 to 2018, Elgar and Rivola kept 90% of their yield up to a soil salinity above 7.5 dS/m, against 4 to 4.5 dS/m for five others (van Straten et al., 2021, pp. 2, 10); for onion, no source read shows one variety more tolerant than another. No source read shows them grown on the island or in Zeeland: stakeholders in the Dutch potato industry named salt-tolerant varieties as developed in the Netherlands mostly for arid countries, with no mention of domestic use (Aldrich et al., 2023, p. 38). A Stock: a field keeps the variety sown in it for the season, so the hectares hold until farmers sow again.

elements.label: Salt-tolerant varieties on offer
elements.description: Salt-tolerant varieties of the current crops that breeders bring to market, and their yield; breeding lies outside the CLD's scale. Dutch breeders and suppliers sell potato cultivars that differ in salt tolerance: of 13 bought from them and tested in the field on Texel, Rivola, Elgar and '927' were more tolerant than the others on sandy soil (van Straten et al., 2021, pp. 2, 11). With no official label for salt tolerance, trading houses claim it for no variety and only say which suit saline soils best and worst, and salt tolerance is not yet among the ten traits their salespeople rank most important for a new variety (de Wit et al., 2022, pp. 271–272); the salt-tolerant seed potatoes bred in the Netherlands are mostly for export to arid countries such as Egypt and Morocco (Aldrich et al., 2023, pp. 38, 40). Tolerant varieties yield relatively little against common high-yielding ones without salt or under mild salt, and conventional breeding takes 10 to 15 years (van den Burg et al., 2024, pp. 3, 6). Measured in interviews across the Dutch potato chain and in field trials on Texel; none on the island.

elements.label: Machines and storage for the current crops
elements.description: The machines a farm owns that suit only one or a few crops (Bonnet & Tiktak, 2025, p. 45) and the buildings, machines and paving for storing its potatoes and onions (Polman et al., 2026, pp. 15, 17), a store for long keeping being a mostly insulated building with a cooling installation (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 5). Nationally about 1,500 of the 3,725 specialised arable farms growing ware potatoes still had potatoes in store on 1 April 2020, which takes a cooled store, by the report's estimate (p. 7). Machines are depreciated at 8.2% a year, installations at 10% and buildings at 3% (p. 13, from KWIN 2018): about 12, 10 and 33 years, if that is a constant share of the purchase price. Dutch arable farms invest mostly in machines, implements and installations (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19). No source read counts them on the island, where one farmer interviewed names mechanisation among the reasons for adding land (Dijkshoorn-Dekker et al., 2024, pp. 56–57).

elements.label: Capital lost on switching to new crops
elements.description: What the machines, storage and know-how of a farm's current crops would stop earning if it moved fields to a crop that cannot use them, less what it can sell them for. A store's costs do not fall when the crops in it take a smaller part of the rotation: they are sunk and cannot be earned back (Polman et al., 2026, pp. 15, 17), and other paths need new technology and skills while the old may not yet be written off (Bonnet & Tiktak, 2025, p. 45). It differs by what the farm moves to. Quinoa is sown with standard equipment and harvested with a combine harvester (van Loo, 2023, p. 75); adding protein crops leaves buildings and machines as they were (Polman et al., 2026, p. 4), and a store stands idle only once nothing it can hold is grown. A salt-tolerant variety of a current crop is planted, lifted and stored as that crop is, so it loses little of it, which no source read states. No source read says what a used harvester or store would fetch.

elements.label: Farmers' knowledge of new crops
elements.description: What the island's farmers know about growing and selling new salt-tolerant crops, from their own fields, their neighbours' and advisers. For quinoa this knowledge is still thin in the Netherlands: research on growing it is relatively underdeveloped, and a grower harvested 2,000 kg from 4 hectares one year and 2,500 kg the next without knowing why, multiple interviewees agreeing that too little is known (de Wit et al., 2022, p. 269); what Dutch consumers want from it is under-researched (p. 270). Knowing that crops must cope with salt is a separate matter: most of Zeeland's farmers know it, yet still grow common salt-sensitive crops such as potato and wheat (Stuyt et al., 2016, as cited in van den Burg et al., 2024, p. 6). Measured in 32 interviews across the Netherlands, seven of them with farmers (de Wit et al., 2022, p. 266), and across Zeeland; none on the island.

elements.label: Spending on keeping the current crops
elements.description: What farms invest a year in carrying on with their current crops: wells and irrigation, drains, new machines and stores. On Dutch arable farms the main category of investment is machines, implements and installations (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19, from national farm accounts); in Zeeland groundwater may be pumped only through a horizontal well (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 26), which costs €25,000 to €40,000 (p. 49); and most farmers on the island's eastern creek ridges have drains in part of their fields (p. 38). An Auxiliary: a year's spending, what it buys accumulating in Machines and storage for the current crops.

elements.label: Banks' risk assessment of farm loans
elements.description: The risk a bank sees in lending to an arable farm: above all whether its operations will earn enough, over the years of the loan, to meet all its financial obligations, then its solvency and its land and buildings as security (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19; Farjon et al., 2013, pp. 3–4). Because arable returns swing from year to year, banks count farm loans as riskier despite the land as security, and the Basel capital rules steer them further toward lending on profitability and liquidity rather than on the value of the collateral (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 47); financing a new concept whose returns are not yet proven they often count as a risk (p. 6). Rabobank's provisions for expected credit losses carried an adjustment of 87 million euro for climate risk at the end of 2024, set by sector on five events, drought and water scarcity among them (Rabobank, 2025, pp. 246–247). A public plan that may change what a farm can earn enters it before the plan is decided (Water board's plans to raise ditch levels → Banks' risk assessment of farm loans). A Stock: a bank's view of a farm holds until the bank revises it, and it weighs what the farm can earn over the longer term rather than in one year (Farm income → Banks' risk assessment of farm loans).

elements.label: Bank credit to farms
elements.description: New loans and refinancing that banks grant the island's arable farms in a year. Banks supply 90% of Dutch farms' long-term loans (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 20), whose total rose from 18 to 33 billion euro between 2001 and 2018, falling slightly in its last years (p. 19), and they have raised the repayments on land loans, ABN AMRO cutting the longest term for new farmland financing from fifty to forty years, a repayment of at least 2.5% a year (p. 47). No source read gives the banks' lending on the island.

elements.label: Debt payments
elements.description: The interest, commission and repayments farms owe their banks in a year. Interest and commission cost Dutch farms about 22,000 euro each in 2018, down from 30,000 in 2014 as interest rates fell (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 20); on arable farms interest was 8% of the costs they paid in 2018, against 12% from 2001 to 2011 (p. 57). The repayment follows from the loan's size, term and schedule (ABN AMRO, n.d.-a), and banks have raised the repayments on land loans, ABN AMRO to at least 2.5% a year (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 47). No source read gives the island's farms' payments.

elements.label: World prices of conventional crops
elements.description: The prices of potatoes, onions and sugar beet on the markets the island's crops are sold on, which its farms cannot move: what carrying on is weighed against. They form in an international market by supply and demand (Minister van Economische Zaken en Klimaat, 2018), set by the harvests of north-west Europe and beyond (van der Meulen, 2025; for potatoes, Janssens et al., 2020, p. 8). The Netherlands was the world's largest onion exporter in 2016, and by a rough estimate about 80% of Dutch onions are processed in Zeeland (Minister van Economische Zaken en Klimaat, 2018); onions are rarely sold under contract, so their price swings (Bogosavac, 2018). The potato processors export an estimated 80% of their frozen products, and buy 90 to 95% of their potatoes under contract or in a pool, the rest free (Janssens et al., 2020, pp. 1, 7), a contract's base price published each year for the four large processors (p. 11). No source read here gives how the beet price is set.

elements.label: Farmers' trust in government
elements.description: How far the island's farmers expect the public bodies that plan for its water and land to keep their commitments (compensation, their say over their land). Trust is typically created slowly and can be destroyed in an instant, and once lost may take a long time to rebuild (Slovic, 1993, p. 677, from US students rating hypothetical events at a nuclear plant; Remkes, 2022, p. 19). No source read measures it on the island: in 2013, 141 farmers in the south-west Netherlands, 16 of the survey's 142 on Schouwen-Duiveland, averaged 2.64 on a seven-point scale of trust in their water board on drought (van Duinen et al., 2015, pp. 745–749), and one submission to the Province in 2021 says the island's farmers no longer trust the Province on fresh water (Lases, 2021, p. 2). From outside the island's scale comes national policy changed or dropped: plans announced and then changed, postponed or stopped, which the National Ombudsman, from interviews with 32 farmers across the country, concludes has left the government unreliable for them (Nationale ombudsman, 2026, pp. 8, 15, 40), and a gap of trust with 'The Hague' (Remkes, 2022, p. 13). Whether the island's farmers carry that over to the water board, the Province and the municipality, no source read shows: a question for the group model building session.

elements.label: Expropriation of farmland
elements.description: Hectares of the island's farmland that a public body takes in a year for a use its plan sets, with full compensation, by an order a court must confirm. The municipal council, the water board for its water tasks, the Provincial Council and the minister can each give the order (Omgevingswet, 2026, art. 11.4), and only for a use an adopted plan allows, after a reasonable attempt to buy the land and with a start likely within three years (arts. 11.5–11.7, 11.11). On the island it has been used for a roundabout on the N59 (Besluit rotonde N59, 2020, p. 3) and in 2026 for a high-voltage station on a site then wholly in agricultural use (Gemeente Schouwen-Duiveland, 2026, p. 1; Braat, 2023, blad 9); no source read shows it there for water or nature, for which the Province buys on a voluntary basis (Provincie Zeeland, Jaarstukken 2022, p. 4). Few cases reach a court, in the Krimpenerwaard 6 of 69 files (Kamphorst et al., 2025, pp. 10–11), since the threat mostly makes owners sell (Holtslag-Broekhof et al., 2016, section Context of the Study).

elements.label: Farmers' wish to keep their land
elements.description: How strongly farmers hold on to their land beyond its money value: family land, growing up on it. In the Krimpenerwaard, where a land-use plan designated farmland for nature with expropriation as its last step, owners who kept their land and turned it into nature themselves named the wish not to lose it, from an emotional bond with it, as an important reason, for one farm weighing more than moving (Kamphorst et al., 2025, pp. 11, 49, 68); selling land held for generations often weighs heavily, though one farmer's father had advised getting out if he could (p. 54). At succession the farm customarily passes to one child at its low agricultural value, the other children giving up part of their inheritance so that the parental farm can continue (Luijt, 2007, pp. 23, 25). Measured among 14 owners interviewed in the Krimpenerwaard, dairy farms and private owners on peat, and nationally for succession; no source read measures it on the island or among arable farmers. Whether anything on the map moves it, at succession perhaps, is a question for the group model building session.

elements.label: Farmland changing hands
elements.description: Hectares of the island's farmland sold, expropriated or passed on to a new holder in a year. Supply and demand come mainly from farmers, those who need land to expand and those who shed it as they downsize or end the farm, and together they set how much land is traded, its mobility, and at what price (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, p. 2). The number of Dutch farms falls by 2 to 3% a year, mainly as farms end at the change of generation, for want of a successor or for a less favourable income outlook (p. 2). Measured nationally; no source read gives the island's land sales.

elements.label: Farmland planned for other uses
elements.description: Hectares of the island's farmland that Gemeente Schouwen-Duiveland's land-use plan (its omgevingsplan, with the changes it drafts to it) designates for a use other than arable farming, such as nature, water storage, housing or recreation. The municipal council adopts one omgevingsplan for the whole municipality, holding the rules a balanced allocation of functions to locations needs (Omgevingswet, 2026, arts. 2.4, 4.2); on the island all land-use plans of before merged into it when the law took effect on 1 January 2024, and the municipality can change it at an owner's request (Gemeente Schouwen-Duiveland, n.d.). How many hectares it designates for other uses, no source read gives. In the Krimpenerwaard, a municipal plan designating farmland for nature took from its preliminary draft in spring 2018 to irrevocable in October 2021, fifteen appeals against it reaching the Council of State (Kamphorst et al., 2025, p. 25). A Stock: the hectares stay designated until the council changes the plan, which takes years, and leave as the plan is carried out on them (Farmland planned for other uses → Arable land in the polders).

ask actors.for: How many hectares of the island's farmland the omgevingsplan designates for a use other than arable farming, and which changes to it the municipality is drafting.

elements.label: Freshwater lens thickness under creek ridges and dunes
elements.description: The thickness of the fresh groundwater under the island's sandy creek ridges and dunes, down to the middle of the mixing zone with the saline groundwater: 5 to 15 m under the creek ridges (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3667, 3672–3673, 3675, measured on the island), reaching about 30 m under the creek ridges and the dunes and nearly 100 m under the dunes (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). The lens farmers pump: wells are allowed only in fresh groundwater more than 15 m thick (p. 26), and it reaches crops through those wells alone (pp. 20–22, 26, 38, 53); on the higher fields above it salt is no problem, the saline seepage there being weak (p. 31). A Stock: it grows and thins over years (Freshwater storage measures → this lens).

elements.label: Pumping the water board allows
elements.description: The volume the island's farms may pump a year under Waterschap Scheldestromen's rules. Where: from fresh groundwater more than 15 m thick, outside vulnerable areas (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 26). How: a horizontal well at most 6 m below the surface and 80 to 200 m long, at least 200 m from the next well and 50 m from a neighbour's field. How much: at most 800 m³ per hectare and 8,000 m³ per well a year, set at what rain recharges so the fresh-salt boundary does not rise (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b). Extractions rose in recent dry years, and the province and the water board talk of registering the volumes more precisely (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021); no source read shows the farms' pumping changing the rules, the 2026 revision keeping the cap. A Stock: a notified well pumps until the board forbids it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b).

elements.label: Knowledge of how storage works on the island
elements.description: What the island's farmers, their advisers and contractors know of how freshwater storage works on the island: how the soil and groundwater behave, and what a measure costs, risks and yields. The knowledge from the pilots has not yet been translated to the island's soil, water and farm conditions, which leaves much uncertainty about building a measure, its costs, its management, its risks and its gain (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 11), and local advisers and farmers understand too little of how the soil and groundwater system works (p. 12). It builds up as measures are built and monitored, so a Stock. Outside the island's farms, Deltares, KWR and Acacia Water shape it: in the project Samenwerken voor Zoet Water they drew up quickscan advice for 13 farmers and feasibility studies for groups of farms, and made methods, maps and tools available with which farmers and advisers can go on by themselves (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 4, 9, 55). The EU co-funded that project (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, n.d.-a) and paid half of a later one, of Acacia Water, Deltares, Delphy, the trial farm Rusthoeve, three farms and the municipality, which demonstrated and monitored new drainage on the island for figures and guidelines on building, managing and maintaining it (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, n.d.-b); Acacia Water, Deltares and Delphy explained its yield and effect at the closing meeting (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, 2024).

connections.description: Summers with less rain and more evaporation lower the year's rain surplus, which is what recharges the lens. In a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, the recharge is each day's rain minus evaporation: in the year it used, summer evaporation (440 mm) outweighed summer rain (425 mm), so the winter did the recharging, and a smaller surplus gave a thinner lens (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3665, 3671, 3674). Within the year.

A higher sea raises the water pressure in the sand below the clay, so more salt groundwater seeps up and the ditches get saltier; in the fields the drains will probably catch most of the effect (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 11, for Schouwen-Duiveland). The rise in pressure fades quickly with distance from the coast (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3674): in a model of the western Netherlands around Amsterdam, The Hague, Rotterdam and Utrecht, it reached up to 10 km from the coast and the main rivers, and 5 km inland it was about 40% of the rise (Oude Essink et al., 2010, pp. 3, 9). How much of the rise reaches the dikes along the Grevelingen, which has no tide, the sources read do not say. Within the year: the seepage follows the water pressures, which change constantly (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675).

More winter rain raises the winter's rain surplus, which recharges the lens. In a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, the recharge is each day's rain minus evaporation, and from October to March of the year it used 397 mm of rain fell against 108 mm of evaporation (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3665). Kaandorp et al. (2022, p. 11) expect the changing rain to raise the island's winter groundwater levels in part. Within the year.

More winter rain gives the drains more to carry off: tile drains discharge the shallow groundwater quickly during each rain (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3661, measured on the island), and on Schouwen-Duiveland enough rain falls over the year, but a large part of it is drained away in the wet season (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 54). Within the year.

Rainwater infiltration builds up the floating freshwater lens, but slowly: the lens is a stock that a year's recharge barely moves. In a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, the centre of the mixing zone moves at most 0.1 m in a year as the recharge swings with the seasons, the vertical flow at most 1.2 mm a day, and every run settled from saline groundwater to a stationary lens within 30 years (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3665, 3673). So a change in recharge takes years to show in the lens.

Where the lens is thin, saline groundwater lies just below the roots and reaches the root zone by capillary rise. In the island's low polders with saline seepage the lens is about 2 m thick, its mixing zone in the clay top layer, and capillary rise of saline groundwater is very likely now, possibly damaging crops (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3660, 3662, 3667, 3673, 3675, measured on Schouwen-Duiveland); the topsoil there is fresh thanks to the rainwater lens, which makes farming possible, and these low polders of heavy clay make up a large part of the island (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 4, 10). On Duiveland the salt water reaches into or almost into the root zone in places (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 26). Within the year: in a dry season, with the groundwater below the drains, the flow there is only upward (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3673).

The thinner the lens under the well, the sooner the salt below reaches it: in the Freshmaker pilot at Ovezande, Zuid-Beveland, the pumped water grew saltier late in each pumping season, which the report explains by the lens thinning as fresh water is pumped, so that upconing could reach the shallow well (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 67). Zeeland allows wells only where the fresh groundwater is more than 15 m thick (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 26). Measured on a creek ridge elsewhere in Zeeland, a lens like those under the island's creek ridges (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). Within the year.

Holds in the low polders, where the thin rainwater lens keeps the topsoil fresh, which makes farming possible there (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10, for the island): water a measure keeps in the lens reaches only the crop on that field, as groundwater and soil moisture, and lies too deep for its roots at germination (p. 33), when most of the island's shortfall falls (pp. 27, 31); later in the summer the soil supplies a well-established crop (p. 27). The lens under the creek ridges and the dunes reaches crops only through wells (pp. 26, 38), which is Groundwater extraction for irrigation → Freshwater availability for crops. Within the season.

Peat oxidation and clay settling lower the land surface relative to NAP at millimetres a year, so a decimetre takes decades: Dutch land below sea level is still subsiding up to 1 m per century, fastest in peat areas (Oude Essink et al., 2010, pp. 1, 3, 8–9). A rate for Schouwen-Duiveland's clay polders is not yet sourced.

The lower a polder lies, the more salt groundwater seeps up into it: on the island the eastern polders lie somewhat higher than the western ones and so have no or far less seepage pressure (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 28), and comparing the island's elevation with a regional groundwater model, seepage occurs in the polders below sea level and rain soaks in on the dunes, the creek ridges and the polders above it, the two strongly correlated (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3661, 3673). Drainage depth is measured from the surface, so at the same depth a lower polder holds its ditch level lower, which lowers the counter-pressure on the salt groundwater (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 37). Within the year: the seepage follows the water pressures (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675).

Salt in the root zone puts sodium (Na+) on the clay in place of calcium (Ca2+); once fresh water washes the salt out, clay that holds much sodium disperses: its aggregates and pores collapse, with troubles to be expected above 1 m.e. of exchangeable sodium per 100 g of dry soil. The delay is on the way back: structure collapses within the first winter after the salt leaches out, but the clay only recovers as calcium replaces the sodium again, about 0.7 m.e. Na per 100 g a year in the top 10 cm of soil with calcium carbonate, which takes 5 to 10 years on heavy clay and about a year on light soil, while soil without it is expected to recover more slowly (van Beekom et al., 1953b, pp. 225–228, after the 1945 and 1953 floods in Zeeland). Seawater flooding is a much larger salt dose than seepage; soils that took up less sodium recover faster, and no source read shows how much sodium the island's seepage puts on its clay.
connections.simplification: Folds Sodium on the clay, a stock between the two: the salt puts sodium on the clay, and the sodium breaks the clay's structure once the salt washes out. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then −), so no loop through the link changes, and the stock's slowness is the link's delay. What one link distorts: the delay lies on the way back only, the structure collapsing within the first winter after the salt leaches out and recovering over years, while the link draws one delay for both ways.

connections.description: Upward saline seepage keeps the rainwater lens thin: the larger the seepage flux, the higher the lens's mixing zone, and in the island's seepage areas the lens is mostly under 2 m, its mixing zone in the clay top layer (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3660, 3673–3675, measured on the island; Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). Years, so a delay: in a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, every run settled to a stationary lens within 30 years (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3665).

Rain recharges the lens only once it has soaked into the soil. Before the floods, Zeeland's well-drained clay let the winter's rain surplus soak through almost completely; once sodium had broken down the structure of the topsoil, it became impervious and sticky when wet, part of the rain ran off over the surface and pools stood on the land, the more so the heavier the clay (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 157; 1953b, p. 233, measured in the flooded polders of Zeeland, by R1's own mechanism). Within the year: the structure a soil has in a winter sets how much of that winter's rain soaks in. Whether what soaks in reaches the lens or leaves through the drains is set by the drainage depth and the seepage (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3674).

A seedbed in soil with its structure lets the crops germinate better, with less resowing, and yields rise, most for crops sensitive to structure: on flooded clay in Zeeland, plots whose structure gypsum restored yielded up to 15% more sugar beet, 8% more onions and, on heavy clay, up to twice the summer barley, while cereals on light soil gained little (van Beekom et al., 1953b, p. 234, Table 9). Part of the gain is the longer time to work the soil, the link through Spring workability of the fields. Within the year.

Fresh water supplied from outside adds to what crops can draw on: the island's farming depends on the rain that falls and is stored in the root zone or underground, and none is brought in (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 4), which leaves farms short of water in dry periods (p. 8). Within the season.

Active infiltration adds winter water to the lens, on the creek ridges, the dunes and where a sand layer lies under the clay: the creek-ridge infiltration system raises the groundwater through the drains in winter so the lens grows, and the Freshmaker and underground storage inject winter water through a deep drain or a well, all to pump in summer (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 20–22, 38, for the island). What limits it on most of the island is fresh water to infiltrate, since the surface water is mostly saline and drain water the likeliest source (pp. 38, 43, 55), and the permit (pp. 26, 45). Years to a decade, so a delay: on the island's own creek ridge, infiltration with controlled drainage added about 60,000 m³ of fresh water under a 9.5-ha field in ten years and thickened the lens by up to 3.5 m (p. 44, a groundwater model of 2020–2050); under a creek ridge on Walcheren, raising the winter water table 0.5 m thickened a 13–15 m lens by 6–8 m in ten years, and the lens had not reached its new thickness yet (Pauw et al., 2015, pp. 1424–1425, 1429, a model result, which transfers since the island's sandy creek ridges also take in rain over saline groundwater: de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3673).

Measures in the low polders keep rain in the field instead of draining it off: controlled drainage and anti-salinisation drainage raise the drains' outflow level, so more water stays in the ground of the field (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 17–18, 29, for the island). Within the year.

What farmers pump beyond what the rain puts back thins the lens, the boundary with the saline groundwater below rising: the water board's limit of 800 m³ per hectare a year rests on the balance between recharge by rain, irrigation water and extraction, set to keep the fresh groundwater in stock and the fresh-salt boundary from rising (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b), and pumping too fast risks salinisation (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 20–21). Within those rules the effects are meant to stay within the farm's field, with in principle no depletion, and Deltares's modelling of the rules (2018) found them generally enough to prevent strong salinisation under and around the well (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021, for Zeeland). How fast the lens responds to pumping, no source read shows.

The more a well pumps from the lens, the further salt groundwater rises towards it: in the Freshmaker pilot at Ovezande, Zuid-Beveland, the water pumped from the shallow well grew saltier as each pumping season went on (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 67). The report on the island's freshwater measures lists salinisation at too high a pumping rate as a risk of the creek-ridge infiltration system and of underground storage (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 20–21). Within the year: the cone follows the season's pumping.

Rain the drains carry off does not refill the lens: in the low polders tile drains carry much of each rain off, and recharge, seepage and drainage depth together set the lens's thickness (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3661–3662, 3673–3675, measured on the island). Within the year.

A larger harvest per hectare raises income at a given price, the price being World prices of conventional crops. The + holds in full where only the island's yield falls, to salt or a local shortage of fresh water. A dry summer across north-west Europe also raises the price, since the harvests there set it: for potatoes, north-west Europe is one market, and their price was highest in the extremely dry 2018 (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 8). Then what a farm loses depends on how it sells: in 2018, higher prices could help onion growers make up for a harvest forecast 44% below the year before, while potato growers mostly held contracts at prices agreed in advance (NOS, 2018), some 80% of the crop at around nine cents a kilo while free-market potatoes reached 30 (DutchNews.nl, 2018); onions are rarely sold under such contracts (Bogosavac, 2018). On the island, a farm with its own stored water gains from the high prices of a dry year (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 36). Within the year, as the harvest is sold.

A fall in the land's value that has happened, through salt in R8: does a farm whose land lost value object harder to the next plan? Through its solvency, yes (−); where compensation pays more than the land would fetch on the market, the concern may fall instead (+). A hypothesis for the group model building session, with both signs as the question to farmers.
connections.simplification: Folds Owners' concern about their land's value, which gathered the reasons for objecting: a fall in the land's value, and a plan that would lower it, raised landowning farmers' concern, and the concern raised their objections. The sign is the product of the two steps, so R8 keeps its polarity, and the concern was no actor's decision of its own. A tenant's concern, losing the lease, was never part of it. What it leaves out: why owners object is no variable on the drawing, a question for the group model building session.

connections.description: With the same debt, a lower land value is a higher debt relative to the farm's assets: land is 70% of an arable farm's balance sheet (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 13), and its rise in value is what made arable farms' solvency 81% in 2018 (p. 21). A high solvency can let a farm borrow more and at a lower rate (p. 19); the debt itself does not shrink when the land loses value. It holds for the land a farm owns: farms owning little of it barely gain from a rising price (p. 26). Within the year: the farm accounts value the land each year (p. 13).

Stricter capital rules raise what a bank charges for a loan: for every loan a bank must hold capital, as the law on banks' solvency sets, the more the higher the credit risk, and the cost of that capital, the return its shareholders require, is part of the interest each client pays (ABN AMRO, n.d.-a). The final Basel III standards raise that capital, EU banks' minimum Tier 1 capital requirement by an estimated 9.0% at full implementation in 2028 (European Banking Authority, 2023). Measured across EU banks: no source read gives the change for Dutch farm loans. Within the year: the bank prices the capital with each loan.

Potatoes and onions are planted and sown in spring, and their soil work must not be done when the soil is too wet, which smears and compacts it and keeps an onion seedbed from forming; a potato crop is best planted early where the soil allows (Verstand et al., 2021, pp. 25, 27, from the Dutch cultivation guides). So the more of the rotation they take, the more farmers need fields that dry early in spring, which holding water back makes hard for farmers who want onto the land with heavy machinery (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021c, p. 44); on Duiveland the board moves to the higher summer level in March and April as the soil work allows (2021a, p. 66). No source read shows how much spring soil work the new crops need: the sign rests on their needing less. Within the year.
A farm that relies on high margins can give fewer hectares to lower-margin new crops.

More income from the land raises what buyers bid for it, through what they expect an extra hectare to earn an expanding farm over the years of the investment rather than through last year's income (Farjon et al., 2013, p. 2; Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, pp. 2–3). The + holds beside drivers the island's farms cannot move: since 1970 the Dutch price has risen tenfold while net value added rose two- to threefold, carried by scale enlargement and falling interest rates (Farjon et al., 2013, pp. 1–2). Across individual land transactions in the Netherlands from 2004 to 2011, the expected revenue from the land had a significant positive effect on the price, beside land regulations, the spatial environment and local market conditions (Boere, 2015, pp. 81, 98). Years: the price follows expected income, and its swings ran over years, falling by half in real terms in the late 1970s and by 30% between 1995 and 2005 (p. 2): a delay.

More income leaves more, after the household's spending and the farm's payment obligations, repayments included, to save for investment; a negative income leaves too little to reserve, and machines then age (Verhagen et al., 2018, pp. 23, 25). Within the year: income adds to the savings in the year it is earned.
Capacity to invest decides whether a farm can pay for a storage measure, not whether it wants to.

Capacity to invest decides whether a farm can pay for the switch (new machines, the first years of a new crop), not whether it wants to. The costs of salt-tolerant seed and soil amendments may not make up for the yield and income salt takes in the first years, when setting up costs most, and the benefits are not always obvious in the short term (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 60); farms whose financial buffers shrink are expected to invest less, slowing their modernisation and sustainability, and banks often count financing a new concept whose returns are not yet proven as a risk (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 6). Within the year: the crop is chosen each season.

Higher temperatures and drier weather raise evapotranspiration, the water crops use when they have enough, highest in sunny, warm and dry weather (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56). Once a crop has drawn the root zone down beyond the water it can take up easily, it uses less water than it needs, in proportion to what is left in the root zone (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8): the shortfall is the part of the demand that rain, soil moisture and irrigation leave unmet, so the more the crops need, the larger it is. On Schouwen-Duiveland's clay a crop that has come up well gets through the summer on the soil's good supply of moisture, so the shortfall falls mostly at germination early in the season, when a small gift of about 20 mm would cover it; onions also need water while they grow (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 27, 31, 38, from talks with the island's farmers). Within the year.
connections.simplification: Folds Crop water demand, a step between the two with no actor and no decision: hotter, drier summers raise what crops need, and what they need beyond the water they get is the shortfall. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then +). Hotter, drier summers is a Constant, so no loop runs through the link. What it leaves out: what crops need is no variable of its own, so a crop's own water need, new crops against the current ones, cannot enter; no source read shows whether the new crops need less.

connections.description: Rain, irrigation and capillary rise from the groundwater add water to the root zone and lower its depletion; once the depletion passes the readily available water, the crop uses less water than it needs (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56 ch. 8, eqs. 84–85, a daily water balance). So the more fresh water crops can draw on, the smaller the shortfall, within the season. On the island's farms a gift of 20 to 25 mm at germination makes the difference where none can be given now (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 27, 55).

Farmers pump more fresh groundwater as the shortfall grows: the water board registered a considerable increase in extractions in recent years, which the more extreme drought certainly influenced, so the volume pumped rises in dry years (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021, for Zeeland, whose farms pump under the same rules as the island's).
