On Schouwen-Duiveland the farms get their fresh water from rain and from the fresh groundwater; the shallow groundwater and the ditches are brackish to salt, and no water can be brought in (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8). They may pump only from fresh groundwater more than 15 m thick, under the creek ridges and the dunes (p. 26): in the low polders the farmers talked to do not irrigate, while on a creek ridge a livestock farmer pumps from two deep drains for grassland through the summer, and an arable farmer irrigates about 20 mm at germination, the report not saying where that water comes from (pp. 27–28, 40, 43). So the link runs where a farm has fresh groundwater under it. Within the year.

What farmers pump is fresh water their crops get: what pumping gains them. On the island it goes onto the field by reel sprinkler or by drip, and the method sets how much of it the crop gets: drip loses less water, so a cubic metre covers more land, while a reel usually gives several gifts per hectare (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 35, in its cost-benefit analysis for the island's farms). On a cluster of three farms on a creek ridge, a livestock farmer irrigates grassland in dry years, in midsummer too, from two deep drains under a permit of up to 16,000 m³ a year (pp. 40, 43). The salt a well may draw up with the water runs through Upconing of salt groundwater. Within the season: within the year, no delay.

A crop that uses less water than it needs yields less, in proportion: its relative yield falls by a crop's yield response factor times its relative shortfall in evapotranspiration, over the season 1.1 for potatoes and onions, 1.0 for sugar beet and 1.05 for winter wheat, the loss small in the vegetative and ripening periods and large in flowering and yield formation (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56 ch. 8, eq. 90 and Table 24, after FAO paper 33, general). On the island, farmers in the western low polders find the shortfall falls mostly at germination, and a crop that emerged well loses little to drought later in the summer (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27); a potato grower at Nieuwerkerk lost a fifth of his 2026 harvest, the potatoes smaller too, when growth stopped in the June heat and the rain came too late, his ditch water too saline to irrigate from (van Essen, 2026). Within the season.

A farm pays for its own pumping, and income is what is left of revenue after the costs paid and depreciation (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 21, from national farm accounts). In the cost study for the island's farms, one irrigation gift of 20–25 mm by reel costs about €200, and surface drip irrigation €1,000 a hectare (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 35), figures the study takes from earlier work, not measured on the island. Within the year.

A supply route carries fresh water to the island: since the island is not connected to the main freshwater system, no fresh water can be brought to it in dry periods (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8). Within the year, once a route exists.

Dry summers lower the discharge of the great rivers, and drought more often brings a water shortage, in which the scarce water is divided among drinking water, nature, agriculture and shipping (KNMI, 2023, p. 42, the Planbureau voor de Leefomgeving's risks for the Netherlands, measured nationally): a route can only carry what summer discharge and the national distribution in drought (the verdringingsreeks, IenW and Rijkswaterstaat) leave for the region, outside the CLD's scale. Within the year: a summer's discharge sets that summer's supply.
connections.simplification: Folds Fresh water available for supply in drought: dry summers leave less river water for a supply route, and the route carries what is left. The sign is the product of the two steps (−, then +). Hotter, drier summers is a Constant, so no loop runs through the link. What it leaves out: the river water left for the region in drought, which the national distribution decides outside the CLD's scale, is no variable of its own.

connections.description: Harvests lost to drought are the reason the farming sector gives for pressing for a pipeline to the island (Witteveen+Bos, 2021, p. 7), and ZLTO's branch there called for one after a report on the shortage (Omroep Zeeland, 2023). No delay drawn: how quickly a dry summer turns into a call, no source read shows.

The body deciding on a route weighs the call; so far a study has followed and no route has been decided on (Freshwater supply route to the island). Years, so a delay: a route has to be decided on, paid for and built.

Clay that has lost its structure stays wet long into spring, so it can be worked only late and the time to make a seedbed is very short; restored with gypsum, it dries sooner and can be worked for a longer period (van Beekom et al., 1953b, pp. 233–234, on clay in Zeeland, Schouwen-Duiveland among it, flooded by the sea in 1944–45, the sodium breaking down the structure as in Clay dispersion & sodification). Within the year.

The deeper the ditch levels lie below the fields, the sooner the fields drain and dry after rain. By the water board's rules for its whole area, the drooglegging is set at an optimum for each use and soil, against both wet and drought damage (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 7); at half the design discharge it must keep a field's drains, laid at their optimal depth, all but above the ditch water (p. 8); and an area 10 cm or more short of its optimum counts as too wet (p. 9). On Duiveland four level areas may run a lower target for a while in wet periods, where the fields' drainage and workability need it (2021a, p. 40), and the move from the winter to the summer level in spring follows the farmers' soil work (p. 66). Within the season, no delay.

Fields that cannot be worked in time are planted late: a later planting date can shorten the potato's growing season, since later in the season it is often too wet to harvest, and where blight cannot be controlled, as in organic farming, it costs yield, so an early date is preferred where the soil allows (Verstand et al., 2021, p. 25, from the Dutch cultivation guides, for the Netherlands). No source read shows it for onions or sugar beet. Within the year.

Where fields stay too wet to work, farmers want lower ditch levels: what deep drainage gains them. In the water board's words, holding water back longer as a buffer for dry times is sometimes hard for farmers who want onto the land with heavy machinery (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021c, p. 44, its management programme for its whole area): the board's account of the farmers' interest, not the farmers' own. No source read shows how much a wet spring raises the demand. Within the year.

The deeper the ditch levels lie below the fields, the more peat lies above the groundwater, where it compacts and oxidises, so the land falls faster: by the water board's rules for its whole area, peat soil above the groundwater subsides in response to drainage, and where the soil is prone to settling the board changes levels with restraint to limit it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 13). On the island it holds Schouwen's summer levels high on purpose to limit subsidence by peat compaction, which leaves the salt-marsh soils between too little drainage depth (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 45), and changes a level in soil prone to settling by no more than the land has subsided since (p. 50); Duiveland's plan changed levels with great care where peat lies below (2021a, p. 67). Within the year: the board weighs the risk by the summer groundwater level against the ditch level and the depth of the peat (2021b, p. 50). No source read gives how much faster the land falls per decimetre of drainage.

Lower ditch levels lower the counter-pressure on the salt groundwater, so the seepage pressure rises; a higher level lowers it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 37, the board's analysis for Duiveland's water level plan). The seepage is driven by the higher water pressure in the sand below the polders' clay (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). Within the year: the water pressures in the top layer change constantly with recharge and drainage (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675).

The board holds the ditch levels lower in winter than in summer to prevent water damage in winter, and a higher winter level would keep the groundwater from sinking as deep (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 37, its analysis for Duiveland): the deeper the ditches stand in winter, the more of the rain they and the drains carry off. On a creek ridge studied for water storage, where the winter depth is over 1.5 m in large parts, the drains and ditches carry the excess rain off fast, and a higher winter level might raise the groundwater and with it the recharge (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 42–43). Within the year.

A water level plan sets the levels the board pursues and maintains (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021d, 2022), after its procedure: the executive board adopts a draft, open to views for six weeks; the general board adopts the plan; appeal is open for six weeks (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 17–18), for Duiveland from February to August 2021 (2021a, p. 53; 2021d). Its levels take effect once the works they need are in place (2025, p. 18): Duiveland's plan proposed studying a raise in 14 level areas, most possible only once the discharge capacity is enlarged (2021a, p. 69), and the works for that were still being put to the island in March 2026 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026a). Years, so a delay.

The water board weighs farmers' need for low levels against raising them: it involves farming among the interest groups as it prepares a plan and weighs their input (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 17), and on Duiveland moves to the higher summer level in March and April as the farmers' soil work allows (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 66). How much the farmers' views weigh against the board's other aims, no source read shows: on Duiveland four views against a raise the plan proposed to study did not change the plan (p. 53). Years, so a delay: the board weighs it as it prepares a plan, which it does when its evaluation every three years, weighing among other things the reports of those concerned, finds a plan no longer current, or once a plan is 17 years old (2025, pp. 16–17).

The water board names the gradually increasing salinisation a concern for the fresh water farming needs, the thin fresh groundwater lenses most threatened, and aims to keep or enlarge the lenses: by not lowering target levels much, since a lower level lowers the counter-pressure on the salt groundwater and raises the seepage pressure, while a raise lowers it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 37, a criterion of its analysis for Duiveland's water level plan). So the more seepage salts the soil's fresh water, the more reason the board has to raise levels, the lens being what it protects (Saline seepage → Rainwater lens thickness in the low polders). On Duiveland the plan of 2021 proposed studying a raise in 14 level areas to enlarge the fresh water in the soil and give crops more moisture (p. 69); how far seepage weighed there against drought, no source read shows. Years, so a delay: the board weighs it as it prepares a plan, which it does when its evaluation every three years finds a plan no longer current, or once a plan is 17 years old (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 16–17).
Rising pumping costs give the water board a reason to raise the levels.

By the water board's rules, the views sent on a draft plan within six weeks are answered in the decision, anyone affected may appeal at the court for six weeks after it, and the board consults the region first so that as few conflicts as possible arise to slow or interrupt the procedure (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 17–18). So objections can delay, change or stop a plan to raise the levels while it is pending; with none pending they change nothing, and they never lower a level. On the island the views on the two plans of 2021 changed neither: Duiveland's 25 views from six people (2021a, p. 53) and Schouwen's 11 from five, which added some studies (2021b, pp. 7–8). The only views against a raise, four on Duiveland's proposed study of one, gave as their reason the concern that flooding becomes likelier in extreme rain, not the land's value (2021a, p. 53); none of Schouwen's opposed the raises in its ten level areas (2021b, pp. 7–8, 53). The region's reactions before each draft were taken into the work on it (2021a, pp. 52–53; 2021b, p. 7). Whether anyone appealed either plan, no source read shows. Elsewhere in Zeeland a view did change the same board's plan: on the raise of a winter level in the Braakman, near Terneuzen, ZLTO objected for seven farmers that one party's gain should not harm another, and the plan of 2015 took a phased raise, its first step only once the field that suffers most has been acquired and its second within six years (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2015, p. 2). Within the year, as the plan is decided.

Seepage that reaches the ditches is pumped out with the rain: across most of Duiveland the waterways catch salt or brackish seepage from below (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 20); Schouwen's water comes mainly from rain and partly from seepage, strongest at its edges and in the low inlagen (2021b, pp. 25–26), all of it flowing to the pumping stations (2021b, p. 24; 2021a, p. 21); and the low western polders, under seepage, drain their brackish to salt water through pumping stations (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27). The board's electricity follows the water pumped (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026e, p. 18), so more seepage costs more, within the year. No source read gives seepage's share of the water pumped on the island.

The rain drained from the fields flows to the pumping stations, which pump it over the dike (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, pp. 24–25; 2021a, p. 21), and the board's electricity follows it: in the dry year 2025 its water systems spent €1.1 million less on electricity than budgeted, for the drought (2026e, p. 18), and extreme rain can raise its pumping stations' electricity by up to 25% (p. 55), across the board's area. Within the year.

The board passes its pumping costs on through its levy, part of the costs of its water management, of which unbuilt land other than nature carries 22.78% for 2026 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026c, art. 2). One rate holds across its whole area, so a cost that rises on the island is spread over all of it: the law lets the board charge pumped areas up to 100% more (Waterschapswet, 2026, art. 122), and its ordinance for 2026 does not.

The levy is a cost to the farm that holds the land: the law charges those who hold unbuilt land by ownership, possession or a limited right, not its tenants (Waterschapswet, 2026, art. 117), at one rate per hectare (art. 121), €115.53 for 2026 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026d, art. 6), and a farm's income is its revenue minus the costs it pays and depreciation (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 21). Whether a tenant pays it through the rent, no source read shows. Within the year: the levy is charged each year.

Once a crop's root zone salinity, as the conductivity of the saturated soil extract (ECe), passes its threshold, its yield falls in proportion to the excess (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8, eq. 89): onions lose 16% per dS/m above 1.2 dS/m and potatoes 12% above 1.7, rated sensitive and moderately sensitive, against 5.9% above 7.0 for sugar beet and 7.1% above 6.0 for wheat (Table 23), so on the island's rotations salt takes most from potatoes and onions. The harm is osmotic at once and comes from sodium or chloride building up in the leaves more slowly (Munns & Tester, 2008, pp. 654–656). Table 23 is a guideline from experiments mostly under irrigation, tolerance varying with climate, soil and practice, and crops are often less tolerant as they germinate (Table 23, note 1): crop physiology that holds on the island's fields, its thresholds not measured there. Within the season.

Harvest lost to salt is income lost: at the farm, salt lowers the yield and raises the cost of inputs such as fresh water and soil amendments, and the damage salt does in the Netherlands is estimated at 577 to 610 million euro a year, most of it agricultural revenue lost to lower yields (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 12). Salt on the island's fields does not move the price, which the harvests of north-west Europe set (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 8), so a harvest lost to it is lost at that price. Within the year, as the harvest is sold.

A field moved from a current crop to a new salt-tolerant one no longer has a conventional harvest for salt to take: the link holds by what Harvest lost to salt counts, the fields still under the current crops. Within the year, from the next season's crop.
connections.simplification: The new crops are taken to lose nothing to salt. That holds for crops grown on saline land, such as sea fennel and sea banana on an arable farm at Colijnsplaat (EU CAP Network, 2023), and for quinoa, among the crops better suited to saline conditions (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 63). A new crop as sensitive as the current ones loses about as much, and R6 does not run through it.

connections.description: A salt-tolerant variety loses less of its harvest at the same salinity of the root zone: in field trials on Texel from 2012 to 2018, most potato cultivars kept 90% of their yield up to a soil salinity (ECe) of about 4 to 5 dS/m, some about twice that (van Straten et al., 2021, p. 1), Elgar and Rivola above 7.5 dS/m (p. 10). Measured on sandy soil, the salt brought by irrigation water: the sign holds on the island, since the trials relate yield to the salinity of the root zone, which drives Harvest lost to salt there whatever brings the salt; the size need not, as the authors warn for other soils and climates (p. 11).

A hectare moved from a high-margin current crop to a new one earns the new crop's margin instead, and the margin of protein crops cannot compete with most other crops (Polman et al., 2026, p. 9). The link holds by what the element counts, the hectares taken from the high-margin crops: the area of a minor crop depends on the room left in the rotation (Polman et al., 2026, p. 17), and in a simulation for Flanders quinoa mostly took the place of maize and winter wheat (Cloet et al., 2024, p. 3). Within the year: the crop is chosen each season.

A tolerant variety earns less than the variety it replaces where salt does not limit the crop: salt-tolerant varieties are usually lower yielding, high-yielding varieties being sensitive to stress through a trade-off between tolerance and yield (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 30). In greenhouse pots at Wageningen in 2024, a salt-tolerant potato variety lost 18% of its tuber weight under salt against 39% for a sensitive one (p. 21), yet on fresh water it netted about €1,800 a hectare with the soil amendment that served it best, against about €2,300 for the sensitive, high-yielding variety grown as usual (pp. 51–52). So the margin given up is largest on fresh land. Measured in pots, which the authors would repeat in the field (p. 52). Within the year: the variety is chosen each season.

Margin given up is income given up, in full: a margin is what a crop leaves after its variable costs (Cloet et al., 2024, p. 1), and the farm's fixed costs do not fall when its storage crops take a smaller part of the rotation, the buildings, machines and paving being sunk (Polman et al., 2026, p. 17). Within the year, as the harvest is sold.

Higher prices for the current crops raise the income from them: a farm's income is its revenue minus the costs it pays and depreciation (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 21), and Dutch arable farms' income fell to an estimated 60,000 euro per unpaid labour unit in 2025 on lower prices, after favourable growing conditions and higher yields in north-west Europe and beyond, slightly rising costs adding to the fall (van der Meulen, 2025). How far a farm's income follows the price depends on how it sells (World prices of conventional crops). Measured nationally. Within the year, as the harvest is sold.
As harvests get worse, farmers find storing water more worthwhile, and those who can pay for it store more.
connections.simplification: Folds Relative attractiveness of storing water, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Freshwater storage measures itself, whose description says how farmers weigh storing against their other ways through a dry summer. The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own. What it leaves out: whether farmers want to store, apart from whether they can (Farmers' capacity to invest), is no variable on the drawing, only in the description.

What it leaves out: whether farmers want to store, apart from whether they can (Farmers' capacity to invest), is no variable on the drawing, only in the description.

connections.description: What a storage measure costs comes out of the money left to invest: its investment in the year it is built, and its upkeep and energy each year it runs. For the island's farms, from a drainage firm's quotes at 2021 prices, anti-salinisation drainage costs about €2,500 a hectare over a life of 15 years, and double drainage €6,000 a hectare to collect the water, with €12,500 to €25,000 for a pump to a basin and €1.80 to €4.00 per m³ for the basin (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 33–34); the creek-ridge infiltration system designed for a cluster of farms on the island's eastern creek ridges, €140,000 to €200,000, written off over about 15 years (p. 50). A year's running costs, figures the study takes from earlier studies, run from €50 for a weir (p. 19) to €1,440 in electricity for a creek-ridge infiltration system (p. 20). The study finds the investment costs high, and for many farms too risky to bear alone (pp. 4–5). Within the year it is built.
The more harvest salt takes, the more a tolerant variety is worth against the current one, so the more farmers grow it, perhaps only past a threshold.

The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own.

connections.description: Better tolerant varieties on the market make switching more worthwhile, so more farmers grow them.

The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own.

connections.description: The more of the current crops' harvest salt takes, the more a new salt-tolerant crop is worth against them, so the more farmers grow it, but only past a threshold: Dutch farmers in salinised areas mostly hold back from saline agriculture unless salt severely hits their production (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 57). In interviews across the salinisation-prone provinces, Zeeland among them, salt in a field was largely invisible and seldom measured, a lower yield hard to put down to salt alone, and the damage not yet significant enough to make it urgent; it would take more dry summers like 2018 (Beauchampet, 2022, p. 216). Nearly all interviewees did not see halophytes as part of the answer, for lack of markets, the soils' intolerance of salt and the hand work they take (p. 221). In Zeeland most farmers still grow the common salt-sensitive crops (van den Burg et al., 2024, p. 6), and on the island the response a source shows is giving up a sensitive crop, sown onions (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 31), not taking up a new one. Years, as farmers come to see the damage over dry summers: a delay.

The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own. What it leaves out: whether farmers want to switch, apart from whether they can (Farmers' capacity to invest), is no variable on the drawing, only in the description. Folds Farmers' experience of damage, a stock that builds over dry summers, into this link's delay: farmers respond to the damage they come to notice, not to the state of the soil. Every loop through the link keeps its polarity and its mechanism, and the delay is kept; what it leaves out is how far what farmers notice differs from what salt takes.

connections.description: Assured offtake lowers the risk of a new crop, so more farmers grow it.

What it leaves out: whether farmers want to switch, apart from whether they can (Farmers' capacity to invest), is no variable on the drawing, only in the description.

connections.description: A better price after transport makes a new crop more worthwhile against the current crops, so more farmers grow it. In France, farmers' low interest in pulses was put down to prices not high enough against major crops such as wheat, and outlets of higher value are needed to give them a reason to grow them (Magrini et al., 2018, pp. 8–9); a premium to farmers doubled the area of pulses within a year, and it fell back the next, buyers downstream not interested in them (Meynard et al., 2018, p. 10); in the Netherlands' salinising provinces, Zeeland among them, nearly all interviewees did not see halophytes as part of the answer, mostly for lack of markets (Beauchampet, 2022, p. 221). In the Netherlands, interviews on quinoa and seed potatoes on saline soil found the lack of economic benefits the main constraint on scaling them (de Wit et al., 2022, p. 276). Within the year: the crop is chosen each season.

What it leaves out: whether farmers want to switch, apart from whether they can (Farmers' capacity to invest), is no variable on the drawing, only in the description.

connections.description: Farmers who know how to grow and sell a new crop find it less risky, so more of them grow it.
